name: Unit 1 — AP Psychology — Biological Bases of Behavior: Sensation

cards.back: The process by which our sensory receptors and nervous system receive and represent stimulus energies from our environment.
The process of organizing and interpreting sensory information to make sense of the world around us; it can be influenced by past experiences, expectations, and context.
The conversion of sensory stimuli or physical energy into neural impulses that can be understood by the brain.
The minimum amount of stimulation required for a stimulus to be detected by a sensory system at least 50% of the time.
The smallest change in a stimulus that an individual can detect.
The perceived difference in a stimulus must be proportional to the original intensity; the larger the original stimulus, the larger the change needed to notice a difference.
A model that predicts how and when a person will detect a faint stimulus; detection depends on experience, expectations, motivation, and fatigue rather than one fixed threshold.
The process by which sensory receptors become less responsive to constant stimuli over time.
A condition in which stimulation of one sensory pathway leads to automatic, involuntary experiences in another sensory pathway.
In the retina, photoreceptor cells called rods and cones convert light into electrical signals that can be processed by the brain.
The range of light humans can see, approximately 380 to 750 nanometers.
The clear outer layer of the eye that bends light.
The opening in the eye that lets light in.
The colored part of the eye that controls pupil size.
A transparent structure in the eye that focuses light onto the retina and adjusts its shape for clear vision at different distances.
The light-sensitive inner surface of the eye containing photoreceptor cells that convert light into neural signals.
The central area of the retina responsible for sharp central vision; it has a high concentration of cones and no rods.
The nerve that carries visual information from the eye to the brain.
Rods and cones in the retina that convert light energy into neural signals.
Photoreceptor cells responsible for low-light, black-and-white vision and motion detection; they are highly sensitive to light.
Photoreceptor cells responsible for color vision and fine detail in bright light.
The area of the retina where the optic nerve exits the eye; it has no photoreceptor cells, so vision is absent there.
Retinal neurons that receive information from bipolar cells and transmit it to the brain through the optic nerve.
The process by which the eye’s lens changes shape to focus clearly on objects at different distances.
A vision condition in which close objects are clear but distant objects are blurry because light focuses in front of the retina.
A vision condition in which distant objects are clearer than close objects because light focuses behind the retina.
The theory that color vision is based on three types of cone receptors sensitive to red, green, and blue wavelengths, whose signals combine to produce many colors.
The theory that color vision is organized into opposing pairs: red–green, blue–yellow, and black–white; activation of one inhibits the other.
Visual sensations that persist after a stimulus is removed, often appearing as an inverted or complementary image after cone overstimulation.
A color-vision deficiency in which a person has only two functioning types of cone cells instead of three.
A rare form of color blindness in which a person has only one functioning type of cone cell, or none, and sees the world in shades of gray.
A color-blindness test made of colored-dot patterns in which differently colored dots form numbers against a background.
The ability to respond to visual stimuli without consciously perceiving them, often after damage to the visual cortex.
A neurological condition in which a person cannot recognize familiar faces, including their own, despite otherwise intact vision and intellect.
In the cochlea, hair cells convert sound vibrations into electrical signals that are sent to the brain.
An inner-ear structure where hair cells convert sound vibrations into electrical signals sent to the brain.
The distance between sound-wave peaks; shorter wavelengths correspond to higher-pitched sounds and longer wavelengths to lower-pitched sounds.
The height of a sound wave, representing its intensity; greater amplitude corresponds to louder sounds and lower amplitude to softer sounds.
The perceived intensity of a sound; greater amplitude is heard as louder and lower amplitude as softer.
How high or low a sound is; higher frequencies produce higher pitches and lower frequencies produce lower pitches.
The brain’s interpretation of sound-wave frequency as a high or low tone.
The idea that different parts of the inner ear detect different sound frequencies; high pitches are sensed near the entrance and low pitches near the end.
The theory that a sound wave’s frequency corresponds to the rate at which auditory nerve fibers fire, producing the perceived pitch.
The theory that groups of auditory neurons fire in rapid succession to encode sound frequencies above 1,000 Hz.
The brain’s ability to locate a sound source using differences in arrival time and intensity between the ears, along with spectral cues.
Hearing impairment caused by problems in the outer or middle ear, such as damage to the ear canal, eardrum, or middle-ear bones; it can often be treated medically or surgically.
Often-permanent hearing loss caused by damage to the inner ear or auditory nerve, commonly from aging, loud noise, or medical conditions.
The principle that one sense can influence another, such as smell affecting taste, as the senses work together to create perception.
The system responsible for smell; receptors in the nose detect odors and send signals to the brain through the olfactory nerve.
A protein released to attach to incoming odor molecules before they activate receptors in the olfactory epithelium.
Tissue in the nasal cavity containing receptors that are activated by odor molecules.
A brain structure that receives signals from olfactory receptors and processes smell information.
Complete loss of the ability to smell.
The sense of taste, involving receptors on the tongue that detect different flavors.
Specialized cells on the tongue and in the mouth that detect different tastes.
A taste associated with sugars and generally experienced as pleasurable.
A taste caused by acidic substances, often associated with citrus fruits.
A taste produced primarily by salt that enhances flavor.
A taste often found in plant-based foods that can be unpleasant in high concentrations.
A savory taste associated with amino acids and protein-rich foods such as meat and cheese.
People who are highly sensitive to taste and experience flavors, especially bitterness, more intensely.
People with average taste sensitivity who experience flavors moderately.
People who are less sensitive to taste and experience flavors less intensely than others.
Chemical substances released by animals and humans that trigger social or behavioral responses in others of the same species.
Specialized sensory neurons in the skin that detect temperature changes; warm receptors respond to increases and cold receptors to decreases.
An emotional response to stimuli rather than a simple sensation; the same stimulus can be experienced differently by different people.
The theory that a neural gate in the spinal cord can open to transmit pain signals to the brain or close to block them.
Fluid-filled inner-ear structures that detect rotational head movements and support balance and coordination.
The sense of body orientation and movement, including balance and spatial awareness, based on receptors in the inner ear.
The sense of body movement and position, including awareness of muscle and joint sensations.
